explanation:
## Reading the line

```cpp
std::string line;
std::getline(std::cin, line);
```

`std::getline` reads characters up to and including the next newline, stores
everything before it in `line`, and discards the newline itself. That is the
difference that matters: `std::cin >> line` skips leading whitespace and stops
at the first space, so `Cache line 64!` would give you `Cache` and leave the
rest in the stream.

An empty line is a successful read of zero characters - not a failure - so the
empty case needs no special handling at all.

## Walking it

```cpp
for (char c : line)
```

A range-for visits every character with no index, so there is no `<` to get
wrong and no chance of reading `line[line.size()]`. The indexed version is
equivalent when written correctly:

```cpp
for (std::size_t i = 0; i < line.size(); ++i) { char c = line[i]; ... }
```

Note `std::size_t`, not `int`. `size()` returns an unsigned type, and comparing
a signed `int` against it is exactly what `-Wsign-compare` warns about - one of
the warnings `-Wall -Wextra` turns on for these problems. The range-for sidesteps
the question.

## A char is a number

```cpp
if (c >= 'a' && c <= 'z')
```

This reads as a comparison of characters and *is* a comparison of integers. In
ASCII, `'a'` is 97 and `'z'` is 122, and the 26 lowercase letters occupy those
codes with nothing in between - which is the only reason a range check works.
The uppercase letters sit contiguously at 65 to 90.

So the conversion is arithmetic:

```cpp
c - 'a' + 'A'
```

"how far into the lowercase alphabet, then that far into the uppercase one".
The classic `c - 32` gives the same answer and hides the reason behind a
magic number. Prefer the version that says what it means.

The `static_cast<char>` on the result is not decoration. `c - 'a' + 'A'` is
computed as an `int` - integral promotion applies to every arithmetic
expression on small types - and narrowing it back to `char` without a cast is
what `-Wconversion` exists to complain about.

## Why the cast on the `<cctype>` functions

```cpp
std::toupper(static_cast<unsigned char>(c))      // correct
std::toupper(c)                                  // undefined for c > 127
```

Those functions take an `int`, and the standard requires its value to be
representable as `unsigned char` or to equal `EOF`. On x86 Linux and Windows
plain `char` is **signed**, so the byte `0xC3` arrives as `-61`. That is neither
a valid `unsigned char` value nor `EOF`, and the implementation is typically a
table lookup indexed by the argument - so a negative index reads outside the
table. In practice it usually returns something harmless, which is the worst
outcome, because it means the bug survives testing.

Whether `char` is signed is **implementation-defined**: it is signed on x86 and
unsigned on most ARM builds, so the same code is fine on a Raspberry Pi and
undefined on a laptop. The cast costs nothing and removes the question. The
hidden case with a byte above 127 is there to make the issue concrete.

## The non-ASCII case

`caf` followed by the two bytes `0xC3 0xA9` is `café` in UTF-8. This program
counts bytes, so it sees five characters: three letters and two `other`s. It
copies those bytes through unchanged, so the output is still valid UTF-8 and
still displays as `café` - with the `é` not uppercased, because nothing here
knows it is a letter.

That is the honest behaviour for a byte-oriented program, and it is why the
statement says so rather than leaving you to discover it. Real text handling
needs to decode UTF-8 first, and then "uppercase" stops being a per-character
operation at all - German `ß` uppercases to `SS`, two characters, and Turkish
dotless `i` uppercases differently from English `i`. Which is the short version
of why `std::toupper` is not enough for real text, and why this problem is
specified in terms of ASCII.

## Counting and transforming in one pass

Both jobs happen in the same loop, and every branch does a `push_back` so no
character is dropped. The alternative - count in one loop, uppercase in another
- is correct and reads fine; a single pass is chosen here because the two
operations classify the character identically and splitting them means writing
the classification twice.
